S.Korea, Japan chip stocks slide; KOSPI entered trading halt

Heavyweight chipmakers Samsung Electronics (KS:005930) and SK Hynix Inc (KS:000660) slumped 5.5% and 8%, respectively.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng index jumped 3.5% with Chinese chipmaking stocks leading gains.

The Democratic victories in U.S. midterms raised expectations that political pressure could accelerate efforts to end the U.S.-Iran conflict, potentially easing supply disruptions and reducing inflationary pressures.
Lower energy prices also boosted bond markets as investors scaled back expectations of further Federal Reserve interest-rate increases.

title: Gold surges past $4,130 as US election sends dollar, Treasury yields tumbling
full_text:
Investing.com -- Gold prices extended their rally on Thursday, climbing above $4,130 an ounce as the Democratic election victory continued to weigh on the U.S. dollar and Treasury yields, boosting demand for the precious metal.
At 23:55 ET (04:55 GMT), spot gold surged 1.9% to $4,138.51 an ounce, while U.S. gold futures gained 1.8% to $4,147.59. Silver advanced 1.6% to $53.0750 an ounce, while platinum climbed 2% to $1,529.40. Spot palladium rose 2.3% to $1,030.54, while palladium futures gained 2.2% to $1,026.75. The U.S. dollar Index fell 0.3% to 101.27.
The Democratic election victory, which dealt a setback to the Trump administration, triggered a broad decline in U.S. bond yields and the dollar. Treasury yields fell across maturities on Wednesday and extended their retreat on Thursday, while the greenback lost 0.4% in the previous session before weakening further.
Lower yields support gold because it does not pay interest, while a softer dollar makes bullion more affordable for international buyers.
ANZ analysts said U.S. bonds also benefited from expectations that the new political balance would constrain Trump’s proposed tax cuts and spending plans.
However, they cautioned that government borrowing has been a significant source of support for gold over the past year, meaning restrictions on fiscal expansion could weaken one of the factors underpinning bullion’s longer-term appeal.
Oil prices remained sharply lower after Brent crude dropped below $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since early October. Trump played down the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran following the election setback, helping ease fears of further escalation and energy supply disruptions.
Gold’s recovery marks its strongest break yet from a months-long decline, although the metal remains more than 20% below its levels before the U.S.-Iran war erupted in late February.
The conflict drove energy costs higher and fuelled inflation, prompting tighter monetary policy that weighed on non-yielding bullion.
Investors will now look to Friday’s U.S. nonfarm payrolls report for fresh evidence on economic conditions and the interest-rate outlook. Signs that inflation is moderating could give the Federal Reserve greater flexibility to ease monetary policy, potentially providing further support to gold.

title: NAB shares slump 7% to three-week low as FY26 cash earnings miss
full_text:
Investing.com -- National Australia Bank shares slumped on Thursday after the lender reported weaker full-year earnings, with higher credit impairment charges and software-related costs weighing on profitability.
Shares fell 7.5% to A$38.08, touching their lowest level since October 12 and sharply underperforming the broader S&P/ASX 200, which was up 1.8% in morning trading.
Cash earnings fell 13.4% to A$6.14 billion for the year ended September 30, missing the Visible Alpha consensus estimate of about A$6.33 billion. Statutory net profit attributable declined 9.1% to A$6.14 billion, below analysts' A$6.45 billion estimate.
Net operating income increased 5.8% to A$22.01 billion, supported by higher lending volumes and improved margins. However, credit impairment charges jumped 85.7% to A$1.55 billion from A$833 million a year earlier, including a A$403 million increase in collective provisions reflecting a more challenging economic outlook.
The bank's cash earnings included A$1.35 billion in large notable items, primarily related to a change in its software capitalisation policy. Excluding these items, cash earnings remained broadly flat at A$7.09 billion, also below analysts' A$7.24 billion estimate on an adjusted basis.
NAB's net interest margin (NIM) improved 6 basis points to 1.80%, as at quarter end.
The increase in credit charges included A$1.08 billion in individually assessed provisions, primarily related to business lending customers.
Business and Private Banking remained a source of strength, with cash earnings excluding large notable items increasing 10.7%. However, Corporate and Institutional Banking earnings fell 6.1%, while New Zealand Banking earnings declined 14%.
NAB said it expects underlying cost growth of less than 3% in FY27, while planning to maintain investment spending at a similar level to FY26, when it spent A$1.8 billion.
The bank had also announced plans to cut up to 2,500 roles by September 2027 as part of a broader restructuring programme, with the changes expected to generate about A$300 million in restructuring costs in 2027.
CEO Andrew Irvine warned that persistent inflation, higher interest rates and weaker housing conditions would weigh on the operating environment.
“The actions we've taken reflect our expectation of a tough year ahead,” he said.
NAB declared a final dividend of 85 Australian cents per share, fully franked, taking its total dividend for FY26 to A$1.70 per share, unchanged from the previous financial year.

title: Goldman flags fresh state buying in China stocks, awaits volume recovery
full_text:
Investing.com-- China’s stock market has received fresh support from state-backed investors, although a sustained recovery remains uncertain as trading activity and investor sentiment have yet to show convincing improvement, Goldman Sachs analysts said in a note.
Buying by China’s national team (NT) through exchange-traded funds began around mid-October and has accelerated in recent sessions, with cumulative inflows over the past two weeks surpassing the total recorded in April 2025, Goldman Sachs said.

title: Tencent shares jump 6% to three-week high after Hunyuan AI model launch
full_text:
Investing.com -- Tencent (HK:0700) shares surged to a three-week high on Thursday after the Chinese technology giant unveiled its latest Hunyuan artificial intelligence model, adding visual understanding and computer-use capabilities.
Shares rose 5.93% to HK$425.40, their highest level since October 16, outperforming the broader Hang Seng Index, which was up 3.3% at 11:12 a.m. Hong Kong time.
Tencent's Hunyuan team officially launched Hy4 on Wednesday, introducing visual understanding for the first time alongside improvements in instruction following, long-context comprehension and long-horizon agentic tasks.
The new model can process detailed images, analyse complex charts and perform mathematical visual reasoning. It also introduces computer-use capabilities, allowing it to interact with command-line and graphical interfaces to perform tasks across different applications.
Hy4 has been trained for professional software applications including Blender and computer-aided design (CAD), improving its ability to plan and execute complex tasks over extended periods.
The release marks another step in Tencent's efforts to strengthen its AI model development and integrate its technology more deeply into enterprise software and consumer-facing applications.
The Hy4 model has expanded its parameter scale to 770 billion, compared with fewer than 300 billion in the Hy3 series, according to Hong Kong media reports. Tencent said it plans to release the model weights and system cards in the coming days, extending its open-source AI strategy.
The model is also being integrated into Tencent's WorkBuddy and CodeBuddy productivity platforms, while its API is available through Tencent Cloud TokenHub. The company is keeping API pricing unchanged from the Hy4 preview version.
Tencent said it restricted Hy4's cybersecurity training to defensive applications, such as identifying and fixing software vulnerabilities, excluding material that could help users build hacking tools or break into systems.
The launch comes as Chinese technology companies accelerate development of generative AI models to compete with leading US developers. Tencent has been releasing major Hunyuan model updates approximately every two months since rebuilding its AI infrastructure in February, according to Caixin.

title: Australia’s 188-year-old retailer David Jones enters administration, faces sale
full_text:
By Renju Jose
SYDNEY, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Australia’s 188-year-old department store chain, David Jones, was placed into voluntary administration on Thursday, as rising costs, sluggish retail sales and supply chain pressures weighed on its business.
David Jones stores will continue to operate under the control of FTI Consulting, the appointed receivers, while the firm reviews current operations.
McGrathNicol has been appointed as voluntary administrators.
"A transaction process seeking offers for a recapitalisation of the business or a sale as a going concern will commence immediately, and will be managed by McGrathNicol," FTI Consulting and McGrathNicol said in a joint statement.
"We will manage this process carefully, mindful of the impact on some stakeholders but also recognising the need for difficult decisions."
Founded in Sydney in 1838 by Welsh immigrant David Jones, the upscale retailer describes itself as the world’s oldest continuously operating department store.
With about 6,000 employees across 38 stores in Australia and New Zealand, David Jones is one of Australia’s most recognisable brands and predates London’s Harrods by more than a decade.
For generations, Australian shoppers have turned to David Jones for clothing and accessories for milestone occasions, from formal wear to school and graduation attire.
However, like overseas counterparts, the retailer has struggled for more than a decade as the rise of online shopping and competition from fast-fashion chains have steadily eroded its traditional department store business model.
Its latest owner was private equity firm Anchorage Capital Partners, which bought it from South African retailer Woolworths in 2022 for a price media reported at the time was about A$100 million ($70.09 million).
David Jones CEO Erica Berchtold said the retailer had "a well-developed plan on how to reset the business for the future."
She added that the company would work with the administrators, receivers and its secured lender during the voluntary administration process, Australia’s closest equivalent to Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
Luxury US department store owner Saks Global, which battled similar retail trends, emerged from Chapter 11 in June after nearly five months with fewer than half of its previous stores and a quarter of its debt.
Scentre Group, which owns and operates Westfield shopping centres in Australia and New Zealand, offered a lifeline to David Jones, but it was rejected by Anchorage Capital, ABC News reported, citing Scentre CEO Elliott Rusanow.
David Jones has stores at 17 Westfield locations.
In a statement to the Australian Securities Exchange on Wednesday, Scentre said David Jones had paid rent up to September 30.
($1 = 1.4267 Australian dollars)

title: Japan services PMI grows for fifth straight month in October

The S&P Global final Japan Services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3 in September. The reading came in below the flash estimate of 52.0. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while below 50 signals contraction.
New orders increased for the 28th consecutive month, with the growth rate accelerating from September. Companies reported stronger domestic demand, new clients and business development efforts as contributing factors.

Cost pressures continued to ease, with input price inflation slowing for the fourth straight month to an eight-month low. Output price inflation also moderated, though prices have risen every month for the past four and a half years.
Business confidence fell to its lowest level since March. Companies cited concerns over inflation, an aging population and labor shortages as factors that tempered optimism about growth in the defense and technology sectors, business expansion plans and increased tourism.
Japan’s composite PMI index declined to 52.1 from 52.3, representing the softest growth pace since May. Stronger growth in services activity was offset by a slowdown in manufacturing output.

title: Democrats vow to rein in Trump as he shows off White House ballroom
full_text:
By Gram Slattery, David Morgan and Jason Lange
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Democrats vowed to use their resounding midterm victory to rein in President Donald Trump, setting up two years of possible deadlock in Washington, as Trump spent his first post-election appearance showing off his under-construction White House ballroom.
A wave of anger over Trump’s policies, particularly the US-Iran war’s role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54-44. Democrats also gained at least 30 seats in the House of Representatives.
It will be the first time that Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Wednesday that the incoming majority would be focused on affordability and accountability.
"We don’t work for Donald Trump," Jeffries, a New York lawmaker who is on track to become the first Black speaker of the House, told reporters on Wednesday. "We work for the American people. And the days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over."
’FOR ME, IT’S RELAXING’
Trump, who had devoted his last pre-election public appearance on Monday to talking about his renovations of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, called in reporters on the morning after his party’s sweeping midterm defeat to show off the ballroom he is building at the White House.
"When I get criticized, like, ’Why are you working on the White House?’ I’m doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America, and it’s got to be pristine, it’s got to be perfect," Trump said. "For me, it’s relaxing."
He turned only briefly to the elections during his nearly hour-long appearance, telling reporters, "I’ll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto."
Trump had cast the midterm elections as a referendum on the first half of his second four-year stint in the White House, repeatedly urging his Republican base to "pretend I’m on the ballot," a message that Democratic Party leaders were happy to amplify.
The result: voters in conservative strongholds who propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Trump’s stewardship of the country.
In Texas, the biggest Republican-led state before Tuesday, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning their first Senate seat there since 1988 and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott.
Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate.
WAITING ON ALASKA, MISSISSIPPI
Extremely close Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remained uncalled as of Wednesday, leaving open the possibility that the Democrats’ majority could increase by two more seats to 56-44.
The Alaska race may not be called for more than a week because of ranked-choice tabulation, while the timeline for a decision in Mississippi remained unclear.
Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.
The Democratic victory is fueling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court’s two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its conservative majority.
In the meantime, Republicans hold the reins and will have at least one must-pass piece of legislation ahead – a measure to fund the federal government past December – that they could use to enact conservative priorities during the so-called lame-duck period.
The loss also upended Republicans’ House leadership, with House Speaker Mike Johnson saying he would not continue to lead his caucus next year.
Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, acknowledged the war with Iran had played a role in his party’s losses but stood by his decision.
Vice President JD Vance, who may run as a successor to Trump in the 2028 election, piled blame on his boss’s decision to attack Iran in February.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote in a long social media post. "The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay."
’EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT’
Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump’s expensive tariffs on imports, some of which were ruled to be an illegal tax by the courts, and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House.
Republicans, led by Trump, accused Democrats of being out of step with voters on transgender people’s rights and other social issues, portraying them as radical and extreme. Voters made it clear they were more concerned with pocketbook issues.
"This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans," Republican Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said in public remarks analyzing the results.
The Democratic wave flooded huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in 99% of the approximately 2,100 counties where most votes had been counted as of Wednesday morning, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today.

title: Nintendo first-half profit rises 11% as software sales offset weaker hardware
full_text:
Investing.com -- Nintendo reported higher first-half profit as strong software sales and a refund of U.S. tariffs helped lift operating earnings, offsetting lower hardware sales, while the Japanese videogame maker maintained its full-year financial forecast.
Profit attributable rose 11% to ¥220.92 billion for the six months ended September 30, compared with ¥198.94 billion a year earlier. Revenue fell 12.1% to ¥966.04 billion, while operating profit jumped 49.1% to ¥216.5 billion from ¥145.18 billion.
Nintendo said operating profit benefited from steady software sales, which accounted for a larger proportion of total revenue, as well as a first-quarter refund of U.S. tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act that had previously been recorded as cost of sales.
Nintendo Switch 2 hardware sales reached 6.49 million units during the first half, while software sales totalled 24.49 million units. Sales of the original Nintendo Switch hardware reached 1.27 million units, while software sales totalled 65.73 million units. Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream and Rhythm Heaven Groove sold 8.81 million and 2.89 million units, respectively.
Digital sales increased 60.5% to ¥249.6 billion, mainly reflecting higher sales of downloadable versions of packaged software. Revenue from intellectual property-related businesses climbed 87.9% to ¥62.7 billion, supported by strong audience engagement with The Super Mario Galaxy Movie.
Nintendo left its full-year financial forecast unchanged, expecting revenue of ¥2.05 trillion for the year ending March 2027, down 11.4% from the previous year. Operating profit is forecast at ¥370 billion, up 2.7%, while ordinary profit is expected to fall 20.7% to ¥430 billion. Profit attributable is projected to decline 26.9% to ¥310 billion.
The company set an interim dividend of ¥76 per share and forecast a year-end payout of ¥86, bringing its expected annual dividend to ¥162 per share, compared with ¥219 in the previous financial year.
Nintendo said it aims to expand the installed base of Switch 2 by increasing sales of existing titles and continuing to introduce new games. Upcoming releases include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Metroid Ravenous.

title: China says US farm purchases hinge on tariff-cut deal
full_text:
BEIJING, Nov 5 (Reuters) - China is open to buying US farm goods, but only on the condition that the two sides reach an agreement on reciprocal tariff cuts, the commerce ministry said on Thursday.
Following a September summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a $60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly $17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, though the plan has yet to be finalised.
"China hopes the United States will work with China to create favourable conditions for agricultural trade between the two countries through measures such as jointly lowering tariffs, reducing non-tariff barriers and expanding market access," said Huang Ling, a commerce ministry spokesperson, during a regular press briefing.
The White House said in May that Beijing had agreed to buy $17 billion of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis.
Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made in October last year to buy US soybeans.
China is on track to meet its soybean purchase target, but bought only $7.2 billion of other US agricultural products, including meat and corn, between January and September, according to a Reuters analysis.
Uncertainty persists over when the clock starts on the $17 billion non-soy purchase deal, as the White House has not said whether the timeline began with its May announcement or will begin only once China’s proposed tariff cuts are finalised.
Imports of those products were at their lowest level for the period since 2019, at the height of the first US-China trade war.
The slow pace of buying has fuelled doubts over whether imports will rise sharply this year, adding to pressure on US farmers already grappling with high fuel costs.
Traders have told Reuters that lower tariffs would be needed to make large-scale purchases commercially viable.

title: UK inflation to peak at 4.4% around start of 2027, FT survey shows
full_text:
Investing.com -- British inflation is set to peak at an average 4.4% around the start of 2027, well above official forecasts, a Financial Times survey of economists showed, hours before the Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates.
The survey of 12 economists was conducted this week, the FT reported on Thursday. Most expect price growth to reach its highest level in the first quarter of 2027. All but one expect a peak above 4.1%, and five forecast a peak of between 4.5% and 5%.
The Bank of England will set out its own inflation and growth outlook at midday on Thursday after a meeting widely expected to agree a quarter-point rise in its key interest rate.
The economists’ forecasts are higher than the Office for Budget Responsibility’s projection, published last week, of a 3.8% peak in the first quarter of next year.
The OBR based its forecasts on oil and gas prices from mid-August, before a re-escalation in the Middle East war pushed them sharply higher.
The OBR said its inflation forecast for early 2027 would have been "somewhat higher" at current market prices. Oil prices fell on Wednesday after a report of diplomatic progress between the United States and Iran.
Ofgem’s energy price cap is on track to rise by over 25% in January, and household energy bills are set to jump by nearly £470 to about £2,200 a year for a typical household, according to EDF Energy’s estimates.
Inflation was 3.5% in September, its highest in almost a year. A 4.4% reading would be the fastest since October 2023, when it hit 4.6%.
The most common forecast among them for the BoE’s benchmark rate peak is 4.25%, which implies two quarter-point increases. Traders are fully pricing in four quarter-point increases by the end of next year.

title: Rheinmetall shares slide as investors question growth outlook after second guidance cut
full_text:
By Maria Rugamer
Nov 5 (Reuters) - Rheinmetall shares fell 13% on Thursday, the biggest decline in the STOXX 600, after the German defence group cut its outlook for a second time in three months, fuelling concerns about its ability to deliver on growth targets tied to Europe’s rearmament drive.
The company cut its 2026 sales forecast to about €13.2 billion ($14.9 billion) from a previous range of €13.7 billion to 14.2 billion and lowered its operating margin target to about 18.5% from around 19%.
The company said revenue and advance payments linked to Germany’s Arminius Boxer vehicle programme would move into next year and that slower batch approvals would delay artillery ammunition revenue. It also said not all expected revenue from newer activities, including cooperation with Dutch missile maker Destinus, would materialise in 2026.
Chief Executive Armin Papperger said in August that Rheinmetall’s share of an initial Arminius order could amount to about €12.4 billion and that the company expected an advance payment worth more than €3 billion.
EXECUTION QUESTIONS EMERGE
While Rheinmetall blamed the downgrade on the delayed Arminius award and ammunition approval bottlenecks, investors appeared focused on broader concerns around execution and cash generation.
Order intake totalled €2.89 billion in the third quarter, below sales of €3.15 billion, while operating free cash flow was negative €82 million. Rheinmetall also dropped its target for a cash conversion rate above 40%.
"The Boxer contract seems not to be the whole story," a local trader said, pointing to weak order intake, negative free cash flow and the lack of revised backlog guidance.
Analysts at Jefferies said they were surprised by the size of the outlook cut so late in the year and noted Rheinmetall had yet to provide revised order guidance despite the Arminius delay.
The selloff came despite a strong quarter in which sales rose to €3.15 billion from €2.31 billion a year earlier and operating profit increased 62% to €553 million.
Rheinmetall’s order book remains among the largest in the European defence sector and demand from rearming European governments remains strong. The latest warning instead raised questions over how quickly the company can convert that demand into revenue, cash flow and programme deliveries.

title: Massive market rotation raises question: Is the sell-AI trade here to stay?
full_text:
Investing.com - Tech saw a sharp rotation into hyperscalers on Wednesday, while semiconductors and data center infrastructure stocks came under pressure as a Democratic election win triggered a huge thematic rotation. Amazon rose 6.1% on the session, Microsoft gained 6.7%, Alphabet climbed 3.2%, and Meta added 1.4%.
"Our US desk is seeing a clear rotation into Hyperscalers from both LOs and HFs," Goldman's trading desk wrote, with long-only funds and hedge funds both participating.
"Investors viewed the Democratic win as potentially making new builds harder and existing, power-secured compute more valuable," Goldman's TMT specialists added.
Tighter permitting, water and power rules, fewer tax breaks, and the possibility of temporary moratoria all figured in the calculus. If new data-centre capacity is harder and slower to bring online, the argument goes that hyperscalers already operating powered, operational infrastructure hold a durable competitive edge.
"Scarcer powered capacity could lift prices and strengthen existing operators' competitive advantage, while leaving future-capacity providers behind," they said.
Hyperscalers posted broad gains, while semiconductor stocks fell, led by declines among neocloud companies. CoreWeave fell 9.9% and Nebius dropped 6.7%, with other neo-cloud and data-centre builder names also declining. Memory names including Micron weakened alongside the selloff.
The rotation was amplified by a confluence of capacity-risk headlines. Brad Gerstner, speaking on the "All-In" podcast, argued regulatory friction from the Democratic win could halt 10–15 GW of expected 2027 data-centre capacity.
Goldman noted that figure was already below more bullish street estimates; Gerstner had in September said only roughly 25 GW was realistic in the US. Separately, research firm SemiAnalysis flagged 16.7 GW of planned 2028 Texas capacity as at risk.
"The main point is that the election now adds political risk on top of already bullish street forecasts well above 30GW," Goldman said.
For semis, the concern is not just slower demand but a potential inventory overhang. Goldman relayed sceptic arguments that "there is a risk now is that the semis narrative flips to inventory correction if power/sites lag chip deliveries."
The Financial Times reported that AWS is taking delivery of roughly $3bn of Nvidia GB300 racks per month but staging some in warehouses because certain sites have space without sufficient power, an echo of the 2022–23 inventory correction that rattled the sector.
"Structurally, sustained AI growth requires the cost of compute to keep falling esp. for further major advances and higher compute costs reduce the displacement pressure on spaces like traditional software and media."
In other words, if regulatory friction permanently raises the cost of new compute rather than simply delaying it, the AI investment thesis itself comes under scrutiny.

title: German yields slide to Aug lows as 20% weekly oil crash deflates inflation fears
full_text:
Investing.com - Eurozone government bond yields tumbled across the curve on Thursday, with Germany’s benchmark 10-year yield sinking to its lowest level since August, as a staggering 20% weekly collapse in crude oil prices and a decisive Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections rapidly drained stagflation fears out of sovereign debt markets.
The benchmark German 10-year Bund yield fell to 3.27%, breaking decisively through autumn support levels to print its lowest mark in nearly three months.
At the short end of the curve, the policy-sensitive two-year Bund yield tumbled to 2.984% - cracking the critical 3% threshold to touch its lowest level since October 2.
Brent crude futures dived nearly 9% overnight, slipping below the $100-a-barrel benchmark to trade at levels unseen since mid-September. The plunge extended Brent’s cumulative losses this week to roughly 20%. If sustained through Friday’s close, the decline would mark the largest weekly drop in oil prices since April 2020, when pandemic lockdowns drove U.S. crude benchmarks temporarily into negative territory.
For European bond allocators, that energy collapse has rewritten the macroeconomic landscape in a matter of sessions:
Throughout October, soaring crude and natural gas prices had injected acute stagflationary friction across the euro zone, threatening to force the ECB into another defensive interest-rate increase despite stalling regional demand and weak German consumer spending.
With oil benchmarks in freefall, the imported cost pressures that had underpinned elevated breakeven inflation rates are evaporating, relieving corporate balance sheets and lifting a heavy tax off European household real incomes.
Midterm sweep ignites hopes for U.S.-Iran war off-ramp
The dramatic decompression of energy prices stems directly from Washington, where American voters swept Democrats to a series of stunning midterm victories, wresting full control of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans.
The scale of the Democratic congressional takeover has profoundly altered market assumptions regarding U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East:
Trading desks are calculating that an opposition-controlled House and Senate will actively assert war powers oversight, restricting the White House’s ability to conduct further unilateral military action following defensive strikes against Iranian installations on Qeshm Island earlier this week.
The political shift has revived expectations that Washington and Tehran will now be compelled to lean into Qatari-mediated backchannel diplomacy, sharply diminishing the perceived threat of a wider conflict that could indefinitely shutter tanker transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
BoE’s dovish rate hike expected
The Bank of England is widely-expected to deliver its first rate hike since 2023, sending UK banks rallying on the day. However, bonds were more subdued, with the 10 year gilt yield lingering at its lowest since August touched in the previous session of 5.098%.
The 2 year gilt yield, which tracks, BoE rate expectations, was at over one month lows of 4.72%.
"Ee expect a dovish hike. Our view remains that today should be the last hike for this cycle," Jefferies’ Mohit Kumar said.

Investing.com -- Technogym shares rose 4% on Thursday after Citi upgraded the Italian fitness equipment maker to "buy" from "neutral", saying third-quarter organic growth of about 3% excluding currency effects marked the low point and that growth should gradually accelerate.
Citi raised its price target to €17 from €15. Technogym shares closed at €14.48 on Nov. 4.
The new target implies an expected share price return of 17.4% and a total return of 20.2%, including an expected dividend yield of 2.8%.
Citi said the shares rose after the third-quarter results, which were in line with expectations.
The broker attributed the quarter’s performance to temporary factors, including delayed dispatch of large orders linked to the Sandstone launch and delivery disruptions in the Middle East, India and Africa and Asia-Pacific.
It expects growth to pick up gradually, with the reversal of several one-off factors supporting the fourth quarter.
Market consensus assumes revenue growth excluding currency effects of 6.0% in 2027 and 7.2% in 2028, well below Technogym’s 2023-25 average of 13.8%, Citi said, adding that it sees scope for earnings estimate upgrades.
Citi’s cost tracker shows input costs rose about 3.7% year-on-year in each of the past three months, or about 6.5% including freight, although freight rates have levelled off.
The broker expects price increases to start offsetting cost inflation in the second half of 2026, limiting the decline in adjusted operating margin to around first-half 2026 levels, down 47 basis points year-on-year, before a recovery in 2027.
Citi said the share price decline earlier this year reflected concerns about Middle East-related disruption to freight costs and deliveries, as well as higher spending, including factory expansion in Slovakia and Italy and increased commercial investment in the United States.
Citi’s tracker of seven listed gym operators implies industry capital spending growth of 6% in 2025, 16% in 2026, 5% in 2027 and 3% in 2028.
The broker said Technogym could outgrow the market through market share gains, new products and sales to hotels, healthcare providers and consumers.
It estimates the company holds about 3% of the U.S. gym equipment market, compared with about 7% globally.
Citi cut its 2026-28 adjusted operating profit forecasts by 0.1%, 1.4% and 1.9%, respectively, reflecting slightly higher operating spending to support growth.
However, a lower cost-of-capital assumption of 7.7%, from 8.0% previously, more than offsets the forecast reductions and lifts its price target.

title: Bank of England raises rates for first time since 2023, says more may come
full_text:
By David Milliken, Andy Bruce and Suban Abdulla
LONDON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in over three years on Thursday and warned that at least one more increase was likely if the US-Iran conflict continues, as it started on a path that its main peers have already embarked on.
British inflation is likely to reach around 5% in the middle of next year, the BoE said, more than double the central bank’s target and a blow for new Prime Minister Andy Burnham who has sought to ease cost of living pressures.
While there was little evidence so far of faster inflation outside sectors directly affected by higher energy costs, the BoE said the amount of inflation pressure coming down the road from months of high energy prices required a rate rise now.
"Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase," Governor Andrew Bailey said.
The central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to raise rates to 4% from 3.75%, but in contrast to expectations in a Reuters poll, the dissent came not from a policymaker seeking to keep rates on hold but one seeking a bigger hike.
Catherine Mann, who said last month that the BoE had been slow to reassure markets that it had a grip on inflation, voted for a half-point interest rate increase to 4.25%.
Sterling strengthened against the US dollar after the decision and two-year British government bond yields — which are sensitive to expectations of future rate moves — rose by a relatively sizeable 4 basis points.
"Today’s (rate) move still feels like a measured, credibility-preserving one rather than the start of an aggressive cycle. Inflation is elevated, but the evidence that it is broadening beyond energy remains mixed," said Madison Faller, a global investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Private Bank.
Until now, the BoE had not followed the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and other central banks in raising rates in response to inflation pressures from the Iran war.
MPC DISAGREE ON LIKELY EXTENT OF FURTHER RATE RISES
In minutes of November’s decision, Mann said she was concerned about "non-linear inflation risks" as consumer price inflation had risen to 3.5% in September, which she viewed as a potential trigger for a loss of confidence in the central bank.
In previous months, Bailey had argued the BoE could take its time before deciding to raise, as it had higher interest rates at the start of the conflict than other central banks and investors had previously expected it to cut rates this year.
Coming into Thursday’s decision, both investors and financial markets had been near-certain there would be a rate rise this month. But financial markets also priced in three quarter-point rate rises for 2027, more than most economists think is likely.
Bailey said such differences reflected financial markets pricing in tail risks of a sharp further rise in energy prices, while economists’ expectations were based on the single most likely path, of a smaller amount of further tightening.
"Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates," he said in the policy minutes.
Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli said a further rate hike was likely to be needed in the near term.
External MPC member Megan Greene and Chief Economist Huw Pill — who like Mann had voted for a rate hike in September — talked of a need for "further tightening" and "additional hikes" respectively.
MPC members Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor – who had previously been reluctant to raise rates – said they would need stronger evidence of second-round effects before backing more tightening.
BOE PREDICTS FASTER GROWTH, HIGHER INFLATION
In its central forecast for growth and inflation, the BoE revised up its expectations for growth this year and next to 1.6% and 1.3% — notably stronger than the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility predicted last week.
The upgrade follows strong official data this year, and the BoE attributed some of the strength to spending on artificial intelligence and to a small, temporary boost from finance minister John Healey’s annual budget last week.
But the BoE now sees inflation peaking at an average 4.8% in the second quarter of next year. In a more adverse scenario where oil prices peak at around $130 a barrel compared to around $100 currently, inflation hits 6.2% in the third quarter of 2027.
Under the central scenario, inflation is not seen returning to 2% until the third quarter of 2028, six months later than the BoE predicted in July, when forecasts were prepared during a lull in the US-Iran conflict which had lowered energy costs.
After inflation and taxes, British households’ income from work was set to fall both this year and next, the BoE said.
Healey’s annual budget would lower inflation by 0.25 percentage points at its peak but raise it later on when temporary cost-of-living assistance expired, the BoE added.

title: Behind Wall Street’s plunge: AI liquidation threatens Anthropic’s mega-IPO

Investing.com -- Wall Street suffered a broad selloff Thursday, with the Nasdaq 100 plunging as much as 6% and the S&P 500 falling as much as 3.8%, as an intensifying liquidation of artificial intelligence and data-center stocks raised fresh questions about the financing behind the industry’s massive infrastructure spending boom.
The market’s biggest concern is becoming increasingly circular: AI stocks are being sold, weakening confidence in the industry’s ability to raise capital, just as Anthropic prepares for what could become one of the largest initial public offerings in history. If the offering struggles, investors may become even more concerned about how the next phase of AI infrastructure spending will be financed.
The selling has also spread beyond technology, with investors increasingly choosing to reduce risk rather than rotate into other parts of the market.
AI infrastructure trade loses its buyers
The selling has been particularly severe among the companies supplying the infrastructure behind the AI boom, including semiconductor manufacturers, data-center operators, power providers and so-called neocloud companies.
During October’s bouts of volatility, investors generally viewed weakness in the group as a buying opportunity, maintaining that robust demand for computing power would eventually overcome concerns about valuations, financing costs and construction delays.
That attitude appears to have changed significantly over the past two sessions. Investors who previously bought the dips are increasingly stepping aside, while others are liquidating positions amid mounting performance pressure and uncertainty over the industry’s next phase.
The deterioration in sentiment accelerated Wednesday after Bloomberg reported growing concerns at Microsoft about the neocloud industry, which has attracted tens of billions of dollars in contracts to supply computing capacity to major technology companies.
Delays, regulatory obstacles and elevated costs have complicated the business models of these operators, many of which have borrowed heavily and committed enormous sums to building capacity in anticipation of future demand.
The market is increasingly questioning not simply how much AI infrastructure will ultimately be needed, but how quickly it can be delivered, who will finance it and whether the economics will justify the investment.
Anthropic IPO becomes a critical test
The deterioration in AI stocks is particularly problematic for Anthropic, which is preparing for a potential public offering that could become one of the largest in history.
The company filed for an IPO on October 26 and is targeting a potential listing before Thanksgiving. The offering could raise approximately $100 billion at a valuation of $1.5 trillion or more, according to reports, although Anthropic has not yet established formal offering terms.
The timing is becoming increasingly challenging. The liquidation of AI infrastructure stocks over Wednesday and Thursday is raising doubts about whether public-market investors will be willing to commit such enormous sums at the valuations previously discussed.
The concerns were underscored by Vital Knowledge Media, which wrote on X that data-center "pick-and-shovel stocks have been in liquidation mode Wed and Thurs," with the extremely ugly price action raising "serious doubts about whether Anthropic can raise ~$100B at a $1.5T+ valuation by Thanksgiving."
Vital Knowledge warned that if Anthropic cannot complete the offering on those terms, investors could become even more nervous about capital expenditure across the AI industry, given that the funding is critical to sustaining the infrastructure spending boom.
The observation captures the increasingly negative feedback loop gripping the sector: falling AI stock prices threaten the prospects for Anthropic’s mega-IPO, while doubts about the IPO raise fresh questions about the financing available for future data-center investment.
Anthropic’s latest regulatory filing, amended on November 2, illustrates why the financing question matters so much. The company reported third-quarter revenue of approximately $16.96 billion, up more than twelvefold from a year earlier, but also disclosed a net loss of $23.29 billion.
More strikingly, Anthropic disclosed approximately $895.4 billion in aggregate purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all related to computing power and infrastructure. Approximately $447.5 billion is expected to be incurred by the end of 2030, while nearly $70 billion is due within the 12 months following September 30.
These commitments highlight the extraordinary capital requirements of the AI race. They also expose Anthropic to financing risks beyond its own balance sheet, as some infrastructure providers depend on third-party financing to acquire chips and develop computing capacity.
In its filing, Anthropic warned that if such financing becomes unavailable or more expensive, contracted capacity could be delayed, repriced, reduced or not delivered.
A disappointing IPO, a reduced fundraising target or a delay could therefore reinforce concerns about the availability of capital across the AI ecosystem.
Hedge fund concerns add to market anxiety
The broader retreat from risk is also unfolding against a backdrop of growing concerns about potential problems among leveraged investment firms.
Bloomberg reported Thursday that hedge fund Walleye Capital plans to return part of its capital to clients, according to a client letter. The report adds another source of uncertainty for investors already concerned about crowded positions, leverage and liquidity.
However, returning capital to clients does not in itself indicate financial distress, forced liquidation or a fund blowup. The significance for markets is more about the broader sentiment surrounding risk-taking than evidence of a systemic problem at the firm.
Still, the prospect of additional selling or reduced risk-taking by investment funds can weigh on market confidence, particularly when investors are already trying to unwind crowded trades.
Combined with the liquidation of AI infrastructure stocks and growing uncertainty surrounding Anthropic’s planned offering, the news adds to an increasingly defensive market environment.
Investors retreat rather than rotate
The pressure is no longer confined to the AI infrastructure trade. While Wednesday’s selling in the pick-and-shovel stocks spread to other technology names, Thursday’s decline has been considerably broader.
Rather than moving into alternative sectors, investors appear increasingly inclined to reduce exposure altogether.
The selloff reflects a broader reassessment of the economics underpinning the AI boom. Demand for computing power remains substantial, and Anthropic’s extraordinary revenue growth demonstrates the commercial momentum behind the technology. But investors are becoming less willing to accept enormous capital commitments without clearer evidence of the returns.
With third-quarter earnings season nearing its end, corporate results are providing fewer catalysts capable of offsetting the pressure. The dominant question has shifted toward whether the AI investment cycle can sustain its extraordinary pace and whether public-market investors remain willing to finance it.
For now, the market is demanding more than promises of future AI growth. It wants evidence that the spending will pay off.

title: US hospitals brace for tougher 2027 as coverage losses and Medicaid cuts loom
full_text:
By Christy Santhosh and Kamal Choudhury
Nov 5 (Reuters) - US hospital operators are bracing for revenue pressure from more patients losing insurance coverage from the Affordable Care Act, a potential drop in government aid for treating Medicaid patients and deeper reimbursement cuts beginning in 2028.
Major hospital chains including HCA Healthcare, Tenet Healthcare and Universal Health Services are reporting steady patient admissions supported by aging baby boomers who require more medical care.
But rising numbers of uninsured patients are squeezing operating margins, the companies said on conference calls after reporting quarterly results. Emergency department care for people without health insurance often goes entirely unpaid, forcing providers to cover the costs.
"They don’t pay, so it’s essentially a write-off," said Jefferies analyst Brian Tanquilut.
Some of the pressure on hospital operators comes as pandemic-era federal subsidies meant to lower the cost of health plans under the Affordable Care Act expired on Jan. 1, 2026.
That caused premiums to spike by two to three times for some enrollees, while others wrestled with double-digit increases in premiums. Ultimately, more than 3 million people have dropped their plans.
J.P. Morgan analysts estimated that declining enrollment in government-run ACA exchanges - where people who don’t get insurance through an employer can buy health plans - will create a low- to mid-single-digit percentage drag on 2027 profit growth for hospitals.
HCA estimates the loss of the federal subsidies could reduce its income by up to $1.2 billion in 2026. HCA, Tenet and Universal reported year-over-year drops of 17% to 19% in third-quarter ACA exchange volumes, as patients who lost coverage largely shifted to self-pay.
Adding to the pressure, Medicaid supplemental payments - or payments made by the government to help hospitals cover the cost of treating Medicaid patients - are set to fall sharply after boosting 2026 results.
HCA expects net supplemental benefits to decline by $550 million to $650 million in 2027, while UHS forecasts a $175 million to $200 million hit.
Tenet is relatively more insulated from these financial strains as its outpatient surgery-center unit, which accounted for about 40% of its third-quarter adjusted core earnings, is less exposed to exchange coverage losses and Medicaid reimbursement hits.
Some analysts said the healthcare cuts could be dialed back as Democrats have won majority of the House and the Senate in the midterm elections.
"We see the Democrats as most likely to focus on attempting to walk back changes to Medicaid and the ACA exchanges, but continue to see any meaningful traction as unlikely," said J.P. Morgan analyst Lisa Gill.

Walmsley had already made one big industry leap. Before joining GSK in 2010, she spent 17 years at French cosmetics giant L’Oreal, holding management and marketing roles in London, Paris, New York and Shanghai and eventually running its consumer products business in China.

She has served on Microsoft’s board since 2019, giving her a close view of the company that is at the forefront of AI and cloud computing, and whose Windows operating system is central to HP’s PC business.

title: Chinese firms’ profit margins trail global peers as domestic demand stays weak
full_text:
By Gaurav Dogra
Nov 6 (Reuters) - Chinese companies’ profit margins lag significantly behind those of global peers, a Reuters analysis showed, weighed down by weak domestic consumer demand and the yuan’s strength, which has squeezed exporters’ margins.
Profit margins at Chinese listed companies stood at 4.88% in the first six months, nearly half the 8.87% recorded by global peers, a Reuters analysis of LSEG data showed. It covered 5,209 Chinese companies and 9,733 elsewhere, each valued at at least $100 million.
The analysis showed that healthcare technology, tobacco, software, real estate management and development, and IT services recorded losses during the period, resulting in negative margins.
Elsewhere, median profit margins were 11.5% for healthcare technology, 21.0% for tobacco, 10.8% for software, 17.7% for real estate management and development, and 6.8% for IT services.
Although China’s economic growth rose to 4.5% in the third quarter from a three-year low, driven by a surge in exports, retail sales — a gauge of domestic consumption — increased only slightly, while the property market remained in a downturn that has significantly eroded household wealth over the past five years.
Factory-gate prices in September rose 5.0% from a year earlier, but industrial input prices climbed 6.9%, official data showed. Prices of consumer goods at the factory gate fell 0.1%, while consumer inflation was 0.9%.
Despite booming exports, Chinese exporters have also been hit by a rally in the yuan since April 2025, during which it has appreciated by about 10.2% against the dollar.
The analysis showed that transportation infrastructure, the leading industry, posted a 20.97% profit margin, notably higher than the 16.5% recorded by its global peers. Marine transport, beverages and utilities also had competitive margins of 13% to 14%.
At the same time, industries favoured by Beijing, such as automobiles and technology hardware, storage and peripherals, had margins of just 2.5% and 3.5%, respectively.
Other priority sectors with relatively higher margins included pharmaceuticals, life sciences tools and services, and semiconductors and semiconductor equipment, at 10.0%, 8.1% and 7.0%, respectively. However, with the exception of life sciences tools and services, these sectors still lagged their global peers.

title: Nasdaq posts biggest daily drop in 19 months on fears of AI regulations
full_text:
By Noel Randewich and Utkarsh Hathi
Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Nasdaq Composite ended sharply lower on Thursday, notching its deepest one-day drop in 19 months and confirming it was in a correction, as chipmakers sank on fears of tougher AI regulation after Democrats won control of the US Congress.
Democratic wins on Tuesday, including in states where opposition to new data centers has mounted, fueled concerns that tighter regulation could slow the AI infrastructure buildout that has helped lift stocks to record highs this year.
Nvidia dropped over 9%, while the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index plunged over 12%.
The selloff evaporated $3 trillion in stock market value from S&P 500 companies.
The Nasdaq Composite logged its biggest daily drop since President Donald Trump’s "Liberation Day" tariff announcement in April 2025. The index also confirmed a technical correction, or a 10% drop from its October 6 record-high close.
"Investors appear to be recognizing that some newly elected members of Congress and governors are looking to slow the pace of AI infrastructure development," said Melissa Brown, global head of investment decision research at SimCorp.
"While it seems unlikely that they will be able to stop it altogether, any slowdown would raise concerns because the AI growth story has largely depended on the rapid buildout of supporting infrastructure."
The Nasdaq Composite ended down more than 10% from its October 6 record-high close, confirming a technical correction.
While chipmakers that provide components for AI data centers were among the deepest decliners, other large-cap tech stocks also lost ground after rallying on Wednesday. Meta Platforms slid 4%, while Amazon.com and Alphabet each dropped 2.2%.
Data center companies IREN and Applied Digital fell more than 14%, while CoreWeave dropped almost 10%.
AI-exposed utilities and equipment suppliers GE Vernova and Constellation Energy fell 7.5% and 2.5%, respectively.
Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX both dropped. Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates in the midterm elections.
Qualcomm fell 9.5% after the chipmaker fell short of Wall Street estimates for fourth-quarter smartphone chip sales.
"This feels like the capitulation phase for the data center capex beneficiary stocks, especially the semiconductors," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management. "But I think the magnitude of the moves is outsized."
The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to end the session at 7,353.73 points.
The Nasdaq declined 5.52% to 24,315.00 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 3.44% to 51,523.06 points.
Following Thursday’s selloff, the S&P 500 remains up 7.4% in 2026, while the Nasdaq is up 4.6%.
Volume on US exchanges was very heavy, with 26.9 billion shares traded, compared to an average of 17.7 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions.
On Wednesday, the S&P 500 clocked its biggest one-day percentage gain in three months, as political uncertainty eased, boosting risk appetite.
Some analysts said a divided government in Washington could lead to fewer sharp legislative changes and may make it harder to agree on fiscal spending.
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack and Richmond Fed chief Thomas Barkin hinted at the possibility of future rate hikes in comments on Thursday.
Focus will be on the US October nonfarm payrolls data due Friday. Traders currently expect the Fed to hike rates next month following the September rate hike.

title: Exclusive-AI backlash could threaten Anthropic IPO timing, potential investors say
full_text:
By Echo Wang, Krystal Hu and Milana Vinn
NEW YORK/SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Potential investors in Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO are raising doubts about whether the artificial intelligence startup can proceed with its planned roadshow next week in time for a November listing, four people familiar with investor discussions said.
Investors are pushing for a more attractive valuation to commit to the offering, with some viewing the recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as being at the high end of expectations, the people told Reuters.
The discussions reflect in part the impact of the sharpest technology stocks selloff in a year and geopolitical uncertainty clouding the outlook for new offerings.
Anthropic declined to comment on investor doubts.
The roadshow was initially expected to kick off the week of November 9, Reuters previously reported, with pricing expected the following week.
Anthropic may need to offer a bigger discount to secure investor commitments, particularly as investors recognize the company’s need to raise capital given a record of quarterly losses and the large commitments it has made to partners in the AI buildout, the people said.
Investors are also eagerly awaiting Anthropic’s October revenue figure, which the company left blank in its updated S-1 filing, to assess whether the AI lab has managed to boost growth after a slowdown in recent months, two of the people said.
Wall Street and Silicon Valley were abuzz on Thursday with questions about whether the company would move forward, in the wake of the two-day AI market selloff following Tuesday’s US midterm elections.
A decision to delay the offering would likely fuel further concern over the health of the AI ecosystem at a time when the success of ballot efforts in many states limiting data center development has crystallized political opposition to data centers and other aspects of AI.
An Anthropic delay could also pose a threat to the broader stock market, which is heavily weighted toward large technology firms whose valuations would likely be squeezed by any sense that Anthropic, one of the highest-profile AI firms, is finding it difficult to raise funds.
At one point this year its IPO was expected by investors to take place in October and to seek a valuation as high as $2 trillion.
Many investors remain bullish on the AI buildout, though the selling in AI-related assets has dented sentiment over the past month. Some analysts say that Anthropic, like SpaceX before it, is likely to benefit from strong retail investor demand.
"It’s not like these companies are not going to be a part of the future," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments, a family investment office in New Vernon, New Jersey. "They’re going to become public. Investors are still going to have a lot of interest in them. Valuations have risen for a long time in the private market, and we’ll probably see some pullback."
Even if Anthropic and its investors get together on a valuation, as Wall Street currently expects, other factors could determine whether the company chooses to move forward with the IPO by year-end.
If the market for AI-related assets remains under pressure, the company could decide to delay the offering until the market looks more resilient and likely to smoothly digest an offering that is expected by some to reach $100 billion, the people familiar with investor discussions said.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday evening that IPO investors are skeptical Anthropic can achieve $1.5 trillion in valuation in a public listing.
MARKET ROUT TESTS AI CONFIDENCE
Trading was anything but smooth on Thursday, fueled by the outcome this week at the polls but also by corporate developments and increasing market anxiety.
Microsoft tightened oversight of some data center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN and Nscale, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Nebius, Iren and CoreWeave were among the biggest decliners on Thursday and each has lost half their market value over the past month.
Meanwhile investors fled from all AI-related assets, with the credit default swaps covering CoreWeave and SpaceX alike hitting records that imply an increasing expectation that they could default on their obligations in coming years.
More than 50 S&P 1500 technology stocks dropped by 10% or more, and Vanda Research said retail selling was the strongest it has been since the COVID-19 pandemic.
"We are now seeing something of a buyers’ strike in tech," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta. Tech has underperformed the S&P 500 by 10.7% over the past month, the most extreme one-month underperformance since May 2002, Lerner said.
He described the selling so far as uncomfortable but not abnormal, while adding, "the rubber band is getting stretched."
